articles.title: One Image or Two? What I Learned Deciding This for Real, Not Just in Theory
articles.excerpt: Every tutorial makes containerizing a full-stack app look like a solved problem. Copy the Dockerfile, run docker compose up, ship it. What nobody mentions is the fork in the road that shows up the mom…
articles.body: Every tutorial makes containerizing a full-stack app look like a solved problem. Copy the Dockerfile, run docker compose up , ship it. What nobody mentions is the fork in the road that shows up the moment your project stops being a demo and starts being something real: does your frontend live in the same image as your backend, or does it get its own? It sounds like a small technical detail. It isn't. Get it wrong early and you either bolt unnecessary complexity onto a weekend project, or you build a monolith that fights you the second it needs to scale. I ran into this question while building the DevOps pipeline for a chama savings-group app, and the answer I landed on surprised me a little. Here's the reasoning, and the part that most write-ups on this topic skip entirely.
articles.author: Jeff Ronnie

articles.title: Modeling the NBA salary cap as a rules engine: dead money, RFA, and the apron
articles.excerpt: I've spent the last while building a fantasy basketball platform (Fantasy Dynasty — my project, so calibrate accordingly), and the fantasy-scoring part turned out to be the boring bit. The genuinely h…
articles.body: I've spent the last while building a fantasy basketball platform ( Fantasy Dynasty — my project, so calibrate accordingly), and the fantasy-scoring part turned out to be the boring bit. The genuinely hard, interesting part was this: turn the real NBA Collective Bargaining Agreement into a deterministic engine that validates every roster move. Most fantasy apps track stats. The moment you add a real salary cap, multi-year contracts, and dead money, you stop building a stats app and start building a constraint solver with a domain that actively resists you . Here are the lessons that survived contact with production.

articles.title: Building a Production RAG Pipeline: Document Processing, Chunking, and Metadata Design
articles.excerpt: In the first article, we explored why many RAG systems fail in production and established a key principle: retrieval quality determines answer quality. We also introduced the architecture behind produ…
articles.body: In the first article, we explored why many RAG systems fail in production and established a key principle: retrieval quality determines answer quality. We also introduced the architecture behind production-grade RAG systems and explained why a simple "embeddings + vector database + LLM" pipeline is rarely enough. In this second part, we'll move one step earlier in the pipeline—to the moment a document first enters your system. We'll examine how documents should be ingested, cleaned, parsed, chunked, and enriched with metadata before a single embedding is generated. These decisions form the foundation of every production RAG system and often have a greater impact on retrieval quality than the choice of embedding model or LLM.

articles.title: Our Dashboard Said 339ms. Every Single User Was Wrong.
articles.excerpt: For most of a day our latency chart was a lie, and the worst part is that nothing was broken. No bug report. No alert. No failing test. The number on the dashboard was computed exactly the way we desi…
articles.body: For most of a day our latency chart was a lie, and the worst part is that nothing was broken. No bug report. No alert. No failing test. The number on the dashboard was computed exactly the way we designed it, and it described a user who does not exist. Here is the setup. We check things from three locations — Zurich, New York, Singapore. Pulling the last thousand successful checks from each region as I write this, the median from Zurich is 6ms. New York is 286ms. Singapore is 441ms. Those are all fine, all expected, all boring — they're the speed of light and some fiber, doing what they do. The chart showed 339ms. Take a second with that. 339ms is not an alarming number. If you glance at that chart in a standup, you nod and move on.

articles.title: You're collecting async iterable results with a for-await loop. `Array.fromAsync` does it in one call.
articles.excerpt: When you have an async iterable — a ReadableStream, a generator that fetches paginated results, a database cursor — and you need its values in a plain array, you reach for a loop. const results = [];…
articles.body: When you have an async iterable — a ReadableStream , a generator that fetches paginated results, a database cursor — and you need its values in a plain array, you reach for a loop. const results = []; for await ( const item of asyncSource ) { results . push ( item ); } That works. But it's four lines of ceremony for "give me an array of everything this produces." Array.fromAsync is the one-liner that's been missing. The spread workaround doesn't work If you've tried [...asyncIterable] , you know it throws. Spread syntax works with synchronous iterables only. The await Promise.all([...asyncIterable]) trick fails too — the spread happens before await , which means JavaScript tries to spread a synchronous iterator that doesn't exist on the async source.

articles.body: At the end of August, NASA is set to launch the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope from Kennedy Space Center in Florida. articles.excerpt: Follow our live coverage of the total solar eclipse 2026 as we count down to eclipse day with the latest news, expert insight and updates before bringing you live reports from Greenland and Spain.
articles.body: On Aug. 12, 2026, Europe will experience its first total solar eclipse since 1999, as the moon's shadow sweeps across Greenland, Iceland, northern Spain and the Balearic Islands. Along the narrow path of totality, day will briefly turn to twilight as the moon completely covers the sun, revealing its elusive outer atmosphere — the corona. Meanwhile, millions more skywatchers across much of Europe, as well as parts of northeastern United States and eastern Canada, will witness a partial solar eclipse as the moon appears to take a bite out of the sun. Live reporting from the path of totality We'll be following the eclipse from two locations along the path of totality.

articles.title: 1 week to go until a dramatic total solar eclipse darkens the skies over Spain, Iceland and Greenland
articles.excerpt: Here's what you need to know before the total solar eclipse one week from now.
articles.body: Get ready stargazers! We're just one week away from the total solar eclipse on Aug. 12, when millions of stargazers will be treated to a spectacular display as the lunar disk passes in front of the sun, blocking its light. Roughly 15.2 million people spread across Greenland, Iceland, Portugal, Russia and Spain will be in the path of totality during the total solar eclipse 2026 , where the moon will completely hide the sun's disk starting at 12:58 p.m. EDT (1658 GMT), according to Time and Date . A further 980 million people — approximately 12% of Earth's human population — will bear witness to a partial eclipse, as the lunar disk appears to takes a bite out of the sun.

articles.body: The teenaged developer of a joke game titled This Game Costs 200 Dollars almost made over $1 million before thousands of players refunded it. 18-year-old Michael Major is behind the viral game , which is actually a sequel to his previous title, This Game Costs 10 Dollars. Major said he created the game as a simple joke, figuring no one would actually buy it due to its exorbitant price, which is the maximum amount of money that developers can charge on the Steam. In fact, the Steam page’s ‘About This Game’ section describes it as “the swindle to end all swindles,” with Major writing, “I know some people will buy this game out of sheer curiosity, and I highly recommend you do, too.” Little did he expect that thousands of players would actually take him up on his offer.

articles.body: If you're interested in dipping your toes in the world of 3D printing then you can't go wrong with Flashforge's entry level model - the Adventure 5M - as your first 3D printer to start. As part of the AliExpress Back to School Sale, you can get it for the lowest price I've ever seen. Its currently available for just at AliExpress for just $135.06 with free shipping after you apply $16 off coupon code " YUSAF16 ". The same printer sells for $227 on Amazon . You're buying it from FlashForge's official store on AliExpress. It ships free locally from the United States and arrives within 1 to 2 weeks. The Adventurer 5M offers great performance at at outstanding budget price. I would say it is the best 3D printer priced below $150.
